Abstract
This paper reviewed the application of parametric building information modelling (BIM) in bridge engineering, highlight-
ing its contributions to improving workflows, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration, enhancing interoperability, and 
optimizing design processes. It examined how parametric modeling facilitated rapid design exploration and simulation-
driven optimization through flexible, rule-based relationships. Case studies illustrated the use of parametric techniques to 
create customizable bridge components and assemblies, which enhanced decision-making through seamless integration 
with analysis tools. Furthermore, this study discussed forward design, an emerging trend that improved collaboration 
efficiency and cost control by establishing early computational definitions, as opposed to following traditional document-
driven design methods. It also emphasized the importance of open standards, such as Industry Foundation Classes (IFC), 
for information exchange, noting the need to extend these standards for specialized infrastructure domains. Finally, it 
outlined future research directions, including scalability, multimodal data integration, and generative design, aiming to 
fully leverage the potential of BIM throughout the lifecycle of bridges.
Highlights
•	 Parametric BIM boosts teamwork and speeds up bridge design, leading to more efficient construction processes.
•	 Customizable bridge components allow for better decision-making and integration with engineering analysis tools.
•	 Open standards can enhance information sharing, paving the way for more innovative bridge design approaches.

Conventional design processes heavily depend on two-dimensional (2D) drawings as the primary mode of com-
munication for sharing project details among stakeholders during the design phase [3]. Despite the advancements in 
computer-aided design (CAD) software that have improved drafting efficiency, these 2D-focused techniques still have 
constraints in facilitating collaborative efforts and interdisciplinary evaluations crucial in intricate bridge engineering 
projects [4]. Interactions among design, analysis, and construction teams frequently suffer from fragmentation, inef-
ficiency, and error risks due to the absence of centralized data management [5].
Building information modelling (BIM) has emerged as a transformative technology that addresses various challenges 
faced in traditional design methodologies [6]. BIM serves as a collaborative information platform that encompasses the 
entire life cycle of a facility, from initial design to eventual demolition, offering a dependable information foundation for 
informed decision-making [7]. Numerous studies have explored techniques for creating bridge superstructure and sub-
structure elements with adaptable geometries using parametric modelling platforms [8, 9]. In addition, some researchers 
have used BIM technology to analyze the causes of bridge accidents [10–12]. The construction sector has recognized 
substantial benefits from the global adoption of BIM in building projects [13]. However, the integration of BIM in civil 
infrastructure areas, such as bridge engineering, has progressed more slowly, largely due to the unique requirements 
for modeling curved shapes and specialized components [14].
A relevant concept is the BIM-based "forward design," where 3D modelling takes precedence over conventional 2D 
drawings in the design progression [15]. Researchers contend that this method effectively maximizes the capabilities 
of digital engineering by simplifying information flow from design to construction through a shared virtual model as 
shown in Fig. 1 [16, 17]. For example, He [18] applied BIM technology in bridge forward design, demonstrating its effi-
cacy in activities such as 3D model generation, computational analysis, and clash detection. Although forward design 
demonstrates potential, numerous technical and procedural challenges need to be resolved for its feasible application 
in infrastructure projects [19].
Finally, the development and implementation of standards for interoperable data exchanges are crucial for promot-
ing the adoption and integration of BIM practices in diverse disciplines within bridge projects [20]. Currently, existing 
schemas like Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) have limitations in accurately representing civil structures, impeding their 
widespread acceptance and utilization [21]. IFC is a computer-processable standard that plays a vital role in implement-
ing the BIM concept [22]. It facilitates efficient data exchange between different application systems in the construction 
industry and supports comprehensive data management during the entire building life-cycle [23].
This paper aimed to review recent advances and ongoing challenges concerning the use of BIM technologies, focus-
ing on parametric modelling techniques and forward design methodologies for bridge design applications. The primary 
objective was to consolidate current knowledge and pinpoint strategic areas for further research to fully realize the 
benefits of digital engineering throughout the bridge life-cycle.

2  Current approaches and issues in bridge design
2.1  Traditional design workflows
Traditional bridge design is usually done by creating 2D construction drawings [24]. During the initial design phase, 
engineers evaluate factors such as traffic requirements, geometry, and site conditions to establish preliminary options 
for structural type, layout, and dimensions. After selecting a preferred design alternative with input from clients and 
regulatory bodies, engineers refine their calculations using software to optimize sections and ensure that structural 
integrity complies with design codes [25]. Information exchanges among design disciplines adhered to an isolated 
linear workflow. For instance, architects independently drafted architectural plans, which were subsequently passed to 
structural engineers for the development of superimposed structural drawings [26]. Coordination primarily occurred 
through periodic review meetings rather than through a real-time collaborative model. Changes implemented in later 
stages often did not propagate back to earlier deliverables, resulting in discrepancies [27].
These limitations have prompted the investigation of model-based information technologies to address the deficien-
cies inherent in the traditional 2D-centered approach. Advancements in modeling platforms, interoperability standards, 
and collaborative tools have led to significant transformative changes. Table 1 illustrates the differences between tradi-
tional design and BIM design.
2.2  Application of computer technologies
The 2D CAD system revolutionized technical drawing production, mostly preserving traditional documentation meth-
ods [28]. Drawings were used as a reference for manually recreating CAD models or defining analysis mesh structures. 
While more efficient than manual drafting, CAD perpetuated a disjointed 2D-centric approach between design phases 
and disciplines [29].
With the advancement of computer technologies, efforts were made to integrate 3D solid modeling capabilities into 
CAD platforms, yielding mixed results [30]. While data-rich faceted representations provided some benefits, they offered 
limited flexibility compared to finely tessellated subdivision surfaces used in specialized industrial design software, which 
are not suitable for direct engineering applications [31]. Consequently, the traditional approach of developing multiple 
coordinated orthographic views continued to dominate, overshadowing the potential advantages of adopting a true 
3D context in the design process [32].
Separately, construction project management methodologies advocated collaboration techniques to help coordinate 
activities through tools like Gantt charts, network scheduling and materials tracking spreadsheets. However, manage-
ment platforms remained isolated from technical design documentation at the source of the project definition [33]. 
Figure 2 shows the carrier transformation of data assets in bridge construction.
Early 4D simulation tools integrated rudimentary 3D geometry with scheduling data extracted from project man-
agement spreadsheets [34]. However, due to the absence of a foundational model delineating components and their 
interconnections, objects were essentially inert "dumb" solids devoid of any behavioral or responsive attributes. Conse-
quently, construction planning heavily depended on the expertise of planners to interpret disparate design, scheduling, 
and logistical documents, rather than benefiting from genuine iterative optimization facilitated by a computational 
digital model [35].

Parametric modelling technology evolved, allowing for the creation of flexible associative geometries based on 
rule-based constraints [36]. Initially, these capabilities were predominantly utilized in desktop applications tailored for 
industrial product design, rather than meeting the specific requirements of engineering documentation. Nevertheless, 
the lessons learned from parametric modelling laid the foundation for the development of model-based engineering 
functionalities within advanced BIM platforms, particularly tailored to infrastructure projects.
In summary, early computational tools brought efficiency gains through automation but fell short in addressing fun-
damental interoperability challenges arising from disparate data silos. To achieve significant progress, a holistic approach 
was needed to move beyond application-specific tools towards an integrated digital platform that could harmonize 
technical design, construction, and operational functions within a shared computable model-based framework. This 
recognition drove advancements leading to the contemporary BIM paradigm.
2.3  Challenges and needs for improvement
Although computational tools have improved productivity from early design stages to construction, persistent frag-
mentation challenges have hindered collaboration and optimization throughout infrastructure life-cycles. Key areas 
requiring advancement include:
(1) Interoperability: The proliferation of specialized analysis programs, documentation systems, project management 
suites, and other tools has led to a plethora of proprietary data formats. Exporting designs between disconnected plat-
forms has burdened engineers with manual rework instead of enabling seamless automated bi-directional interfaces 
[37]. Addressing fragmentation necessitates open standards to facilitate cross-platform exchanges without data loss.
(2) Integration: The separation of technical performance evaluation using analysis models from the master design 
documentation poses a risk of desynchronization over time, as changes may not propagate bidirectionally between 
disparate representations. Validating performance directly against the computable design model is crucial to streamline 
simulation-based decision-making processes [38].
(3) Collaboration: Traditional project delivery methods have compartmentalized work into isolated phases, with infor-
mation transferred through document handoffs lacking shared access to a dynamic collaborative model [39]. Facilitating 
real-time interdisciplinary interaction within a common virtual information environment could enhance coordination 
and detect errors at earlier stages.
(4) Optimization: The ability to explore design concepts and conduct performance-driven optimization was hampered 
by the need to manually adjust analysis models based on static documentation files, rather than directly interacting 
with a computable digital definition. Implementing tightly-coupled simulation loops could enhance agility in decision-
making processes [40].
(5) Adaptability: The increasing complexity of projects necessitates flexible design processes capable of accommo-
dating changes without leading to extensive rework due to discrepancies in fragmented representations. Establishing 
building information within a digital model structure directly linked to associative documentation could mitigate the 
impacts of design alterations [41].
Model-based solutions have emerged as effective means to surmount barriers by fostering integration among various 
technical software silos. BIM represents a digitally curated master model that consolidates interconnected computable 
representations of design elements, engineering analyses, construction plans, facility operations, and other relevant data 
[42]. Unlike conventional static documents, BIM tools enable the creation of dynamic digital twins that actively simulate 
real-world building performance, facilitating informed decision-making across all stages of the project life-cycle [43].

3  Parametric BIM for structural design and analysis
3.1  Parametric modelling concepts and benefits
BIM represents a fundamental shift in the approach to project documentation, transitioning towards a unified model-
based engineering methodology that encompasses the entire project life-cycle [44]. At the heart of BIM lies the creation 
and management of a virtual information model that consists of computable object definitions interconnected through 
systematic rule-based constraints. The integration of parametric modelling techniques within BIM platforms not only 
enhances flexibility, automation, and engineering optimization but also enables dynamic design adjustments based 
on predefined parameters, fostering greater efficiency and accuracy in project development. The advantages of BIM 
modelling technology can be seen in Table 2.
BIM parametric modelling, also known as “variational modelling,” entails defining the geometries, properties, and 
behaviors of building components based on parametric relationships rather than fixed dimensions [45]. Parameters func-
tion as variables that can trigger associative modifications to entire model sections or assemblies when manipulated by 
the user or simulation algorithms [46]. The modelling approach of BIM technology based on Revit software is shown in 
Fig. 3. For example, by defining parameters such as pier height, width, and cross-sectional shape, engineers can create a 
parametric model that automatically adjusts the geometry of the piers in response to changes in these parameters [47]. 
This enables efficient exploration of different design options and facilitates quick modifications to the bridge design 
while maintaining design integrity and consistency.
Rather than static predefined entities, BIM parametric objects house intelligence to self-modify geometry, sched-
ules and connected components through input triggers following embedded generative rules. Engineers can rapidly 
explore design alternatives through iterative investigation of parameter design spaces without rebuilding disconnected 
representations from scratch as required by traditional segmented workflows [48]. Entire assemblies flexibly adapt to 
conform with engineering requirements or material availability factors optimized through simulation-led evaluations.
The parametric intelligence embedded within model objects establishes relational constraints that govern how altera-
tions propagate through interconnected components. For instance, adjusting the height of a column may necessitate 
changes in beam lengths to maintain structural connectivity [49]. Continuous bidirectional associativity ensures coher-
ence, with parameters or linked properties automatically updating to preserve design integrity. By incorporating model 
intelligence through embedded parametric rules, dynamic runtime support is provided for evaluating fully associative 
behavior, surpassing the capabilities of standalone analysis tools [50]. Simulations can convey outcomes to directly 
adjust driving parameter values, enabling real-time iterations of the model state within coupled optimization loops. 
The automation of simulation-driven parameter optimization facilitates generative and performance-oriented design, 
allowing for the exploration of innovative structural solutions.
Although parametric modelling technology offers numerous advantages, its practical application often encounters 
challenges, particularly when interfacing with other software systems. One of the critical issues in the contemporary use 
of BIM technology revolves around the integration between Revit and various FEM commercial software packages, such 
as ANSYS, ABAQUS, and ETABS. This interaction is especially significant in the realms of structural analysis and design, 
where the accuracy and consistency of data are paramount.

Revit is renowned for its robust modeling capabilities tailored for architectural design; however, it presents several 
technical challenges during data exchange with FEM software. A notable discrepancy lies in the material models utilized 
by both platforms. Revit’s material definitions are predominantly geared towards architectural visualization, whereas 
FEM software emphasizes mechanical properties, including Young’s modulus, Poisson’s ratio, yield strength, and other 
critical parameters. This divergence in focus complicates the direct mapping of material properties from Revit to their 
corresponding definitions in FEM software. Moreover, the differing formats used for material definitions between Revit 
and FEM software necessitate additional conversion steps during data import and export. Such conversions can introduce 
errors, particularly when dealing with composite or layered materials, which require precise definitions to accurately 
reflect their behavior under various loading conditions.
Another aspect that complicates the interface between Revit and FEM software is the handling of geometric models, 
especially concerning symmetry and coordinate system definitions. The node positions in Revit are typically determined 
based on architectural design requirements, which may not align with the precision necessary for FEM analysis. FEM 
software demands exact node locations to facilitate accurate mechanical evaluations. Consequently, even minor devia-
tions in node positions during the transfer process can lead to significant errors in the overall analysis results.
3.2  Application of parametric BIM in bridge projects
As shown in Table 3, it provides the application of BIM technology in engineering in China. The application of BIM in 
these cases involved essential functionalities such as detailed modelling, collaborative design, 4D construction dynamic 
management, and safety and quality assurance, resulting in significant enhancements in construction efficiency, collision 
prevention, and project management optimization.
While the use of BIM has become more widespread in general building projects, its application in civil infrastructure 
is still an area of ongoing research and development. Bridges, in particular, pose unique challenges due to their com-
plex geometries, varied loading conditions, and intricate structural behaviors, necessitating specialized model content 
and analytical capabilities within BIM platforms. Various studies have been conducted to explore effective methods for 
representing bridges using parametric modelling techniques.
One methodology involves defining bridge superstructure and substructure components as customizable parametric 
families within BIM authoring tools [59]. Research developed Revit reinforcement families for precast box girders enabling 
parametric definition of segment dimensions, post-tensioning layout and concrete properties [60]. A Dynamo script 
automated segment design by optimizing post-tensioning forces against balance requirements. Similar families imple-
mented in Revit modeled a composite trapezoidal box girder suitable for rapid deployment on infrastructure projects [61].

Additional initiatives have established adaptable parametric bridge elements using Generative Components, Direct 
Dimensions or Grasshopper plugins, capitalizing on their algorithmic modelling capabilities in contrast to the limita-
tions of BIM authoring software [62]. In one study, columns, rafters, purlins, and claddings were defined as parametric

assemble steel portal frame components optimized for construction sequences. Furthermore, Grasshopper was employed 
to generate 3D bridge models from 2D structural drawings imported into Rhino, facilitating the swift assessment of 
various construction sequences [55].
Beyond modelling individual parts, comprehensive bridge models were algorithmically developed. Using shape gram-
mars, Grasshopper dynamically defined a continuous truss bridge topologically, adjusting node positions and member 
lengths to ensure connectivity under geometric variations [64, 65]. Yang, Lin [66] parameterized a truss bridge spanning 
multiple sections and cross-sections to enable thorough topology optimization. Their algorithmic assembly method 
specified all nodes and connections, which could be adjusted through a limited set of controllable design variables, 
facilitating extensive multi-objective optimization.
Specialized analysis models benefited from tight integration with parametric BIM systems. Dynamo Python scripts 
extracted structural parameters like member sizes from a Revit bridge model to automatically generate an analytical 
model compatible with FEM software [67]. Associativity ensured consistency as the BIM geometry or properties updated. 
The FEM was solved then directly integrated results back into the BIM for feedback-based design iterations.
Similar approaches coupled Grasshopper/Rhino parametric models as a front-end representation to generate analytical 
meshes for simulation software [68]. Parameter changes were automatically propagated between digital twin instances 
facilitating rapid performance-driven explorations of multi-objective bridge topologies. Other efforts imported analytical 
results mappings directly back into Grasshopper for stress visualization augmenting the core bridge definition model [69].
In summary, these studies illustrate how parametric modelling facilitates innovative, optimization-centered workflows 
for data-informed bridge design evolution. Through the algorithmic definition of customizable intelligent components 
interconnected with high-fidelity solvers, BIM platforms hold the potential to enhance efficiency in innovation and 
decision-making processes. Advancements in seamlessly integrating domain expertise from engineering, fabrication, 
and construction represent significant research frontiers.
3.3  Integration of BIM with analysis tools
Although the application of parametric BIM holds great potential for the flexible creation and simulation of digital twins 
for bridges, fully harnessing the capabilities of model-based design necessitates smooth, bidirectional interfaces with 
top-tier analysis tools. Conventional data exchanges between distinct modelling platforms have historically required 
manual reformatting, leading to decreased efficiency gains. Researchers have delved into methodologies aimed at more 
closely integrating technical simulations within the BIM environment to address these challenges.
BIM technology showcases a range of functionalities and characteristics across different software platforms, each 
offering distinct advantages along with certain limitations [70]. Modelling tools such as Revit, CATIA, Microstation, and 
ArchiCAD excel in integration and parametric modelling capabilities, making them well-suited for intricate geometric 
designs. However, challenges may arise in performance when handling large-scale projects, and tools like CATIA may 
demand extensive skill development and training due to their intricate interfaces. Collision detection tools such as

Sustainability analysis tools such as Echotect, IES, Green Building Studio, and PKPM offer comprehensive energy and 
environmental simulations, particularly excelling in the early stages of design. However, their support for localized stand-

PKPM excel in high-rise and complex structural design. PKPM, in particular, offers significant advantages in compliance 
with local standards, although its application in international contexts is somewhat constrained.
For mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) analysis, tools like Designmaster, IES Virtual Environment, and Trane 
Trace provide comprehensive system analysis and precise energy consumption predictions [72]. However, their lack of 
localization support and steep learning curves may impede widespread adoption. Operation management platforms 
such as ArchiBUS and FacilityONE excel in life-cycle management and post-construction optimization, although they 
may have limited integration with modelling tools. Cost management tools like Innovaya and Solibri enable rapid and 
accurate quantity takeoff and cost analysis, but their standalone functionality is relatively narrow, necessitating support 
from other software. Publication review tools such as Design Review and Adobe 3D PDF facilitate 3D model sharing, 
annotation, and collaboration, but they may lack advanced editing or model modification features.
Despite their individual limitations, these tools achieve effective interoperability through unified data formats, such 
as IFC files, and collaborative fa-tigue platforms like BIM 360 [73]. This compatibility enables seamless data sharing and 
coordination across modelling, analysis, and management processes, empowering BIM technology to deliver precise 
models and accurate quantifications for real-world engineering projects. This, in turn, enhances design accuracy and 
management efficiency.
To further enhance this integration, researchers have developed innovative solutions to streamline the conversion of 
BIM models into analytical representations, bridging gaps between design and analysis workflows.
One approach involved the development of geometry processing routines to directly convert BIM models into com-
patible analytical representations. A Grasshopper plugin was utilized to extract the geometric characteristics of bridge 
elements modeled in Revit (using Dynamo), automatically generating standardized Input Deck files for the ANSYS FEM 
analysis solver [74]. In another study, the OpenSeesPy bridge plugin was created, allowing for the direct generation 
of an OpenSees analytical model from a parametric BIM defined in Rhino/Grasshopper [75]. The use of OpenSeesPy in 
a BIM environment can be useful for scenario evaluations of structural degradation as in case of corrosion [76]. These 
approaches significantly reduced the need for manual remeshing, thereby enhancing synchronization between the 
models.
To leverage BIM authoring functions, Bentley Systems developed a FEM analysis tool natively integrated within their 
ProjectWise platform [77]. Models maintained bi-directional associativity allowing users to directly modify material 
properties or member sizes within the BIM and observe simulation response in real-time without file handoffs. Similar 
efforts developed FEM modules directly as plugins within Revit leveraging its rule-based modelling paradigm [78].
Going further, research coupled generative design optimization algorithms directly to structural performance simula-
tions. An automatic optimization framework dynamically regenerated Grasshopper definitions consistent with changes 
from a genetic optimization routine evaluating bridge topologies using Galapagos solvers [79]. Updates immediately 
modulated the parametric model driving convergent results. Other efforts implemented an inverse design approach to 
optimize modular bridge parameters like span arrangements and member sizing via an iterative generative design loop 
integrating FEM-driven performance feedback [61, 80].
Linking machine learning with simulations also showed potential [81]. Abbas, Kavrakov [82] utilized an artificial neural 
network (ANN) to predict the dynamic response of bridge deck panels in significantly less computational time compared 
to traditional FEM. The surrogate model was incorporated into parametric BIM definitions to rapidly screen design varia-
tions during conceptual exploration guided by deflection criteria rather than wait for computationally-expensive direct 
simulations. ANN and explainability approaches could be integrated in a BIM environment to setup an effective SHM 
system to monitor prestressing force reduction in concrete girder bridges [83].
While achievements in integrating analytical capabilities point to promising advancements, current research is focused 
on bridging gaps related to interoperability bottlenecks and software fragmentation challenges. The development of 
standardized open interfaces and Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) that facilitate connections between vari-
ous modelling tools is crucial for fully realizing the advantages of integrated digital engineering in bridge projects and

4  BIM‑based forward design for bridges
4.1  Concept and characteristics of forward design
BIM-based forward design aims to streamline processes through early model authoring supporting real-time collabora-
tion optimized around a living digital twin, as shown in Fig. 4 [84]. Validation and testing processes are crucial in ensuring 
that BIM-based forward design enhances coordination while providing accurate, reliable, and practical outcomes [85]. 
Accuracy is initially confirmed through geometric consistency checks, where automated tools like Solibri Model Checker 
evaluate the alignment, dimensions, and connections of components against predefined standards. These checks aid in 
early detection of potential design errors, minimizing downstream complications.
Moreover, reliability testing is carried out using structural analysis tools like ANSYS and ETABS to simulate load-bearing 
capacities and dynamic responses under different conditions [86]. This process guarantees that the digital model can 
withstand real-world stress factors, such as wind, seismic forces, and traffic loads. These validation procedures seamlessly 
integrate into the forward design workflow, ensuring that modifications prompted by testing are dynamically incorpo-
rated into the evolving digital twin.
Instead of producing finalized construction drawings as the initial design deliverable for subsequent teams, progres-
sive design employs a model-first approach. This creates a detailed virtual prototype that is globally accessible from 
the project’s start [87]. He, Lin [88] developed a BIM-based preliminary planning modeling system for residential real 
estate projects, improving efficiency and quality through standardized unit modeling methods. Designers interact with 
components directly in the model composition workspace, using gestures that resemble physical modeling rather than 
abstract drafting [89]. This approach establishes a unified computational framework that acts as a shared knowledge 
base for all stakeholders throughout the infrastructure life cycle, eliminating the need for separate document transfers 
[90]. Changes are integrated seamlessly in both directions, ensuring connectivity is maintained as the model adapts to 
external simulations, code reviews, or constructability considerations. This early integration effectively addresses potential 
issues before they progress to later phases [91]. Additionally, integrated model-based reporting automates tasks such as 
tracking visualizations and coordinating model slice sets, enabling smooth handovers at the end of project phases [92].
Key forward design characteristics include model-centric processes establishing living digital twins as persistent knowl-
edge bases. Global distributed real-time concurrent editing supports continuous peer review. Document/drawing pro-
duction automates from the computational model state. Intrinsic model associativity maintains synchrony under iterative 
change/feedback cycles [93]. Segmented permissions/views modularize contributor scopes. In summary, forward design 
promises next-generation agility unlocking comprehensive model-based engineering across infrastructure projects.

4.2  Case studies on bridge forward design
Early infrastructure forward design prototypes addressed limited aspects to demonstrate proof-of-concepts. As platforms 
matured integrative capabilities, research applied the holistic model-centric paradigm to entire bridge projects revealing 
opportunities and refinement needs. This section reviews representative forward design case studies.
An initial proof-of-concept implemented Grasshopper to parametrically design a steel truss footbridge directly within 
a virtual 3D environment [94]. Standard components populated a library enabling rapid assembly compliant with pre-
liminary requirements. Outcomes highlighted forward design potential for informed early decision making. However, 
scope remained narrow without production deliverables.
A more encompassing case applied Lean Design Management principles to the forward design of Georgia Depart-
ment of Transportation (GDOT) Bridge using Bentley’s ProjectWise platform [95]. Multi-disciplinary teams engineered 
superstructure sections and piles concurrently inspecting clashing regions detected automatically. Reports extracted 
cut lists, visualizations and stakeholder briefings enabling just-in-time reviews preventing rework. Tolerance analyses 
further optimized pile configurations in real-time.
One study fully integrated analysis and optimization within a forward design model [96]. A parametric bridge com-
ponent library incorporating OpenSees dynamic simulations facilitated optimization-driven dimensional adjustments 
across entire load-bearing assemblies through integrated performance evaluations. Outcomes accelerated exploration 
although software fragmentation inhibited broader adoption.
Another forward design implementation involved a PC composite box girder bridge in China leveraging specialized 
programming interfaces enabling tight performance coupling [97]. Python scripting automated generation of jigsaw-
piece precast components from optimized section parameters simultaneously updating analysis models compatible with 
ANSYS and Midas solvers. Stakeholder reviews benefited from associative clash detections across assembly sequences

5  Information sharing through IFC standards
5.1  Overview of IFC standards
The broad use of model-based methods relies on open and compatible data standards that allow easy communication 
across different areas and systems. The extraction of IFC file content is shown in Fig. 5. The IFC specification by building 
SMART is the main framework for BIM data compatibility, with ongoing improvements [108]. This section gives an over-
view of the IFC standards, discussing aspects relevant to model-based bridge engineering.
IFC was conceived by the International Alliance for Interoperability (IAI) in 1994 to address fragmentation imped-
ing digital building processes [109]. The IFC data model was structured using an object-oriented EXPRESS modelling 
language encoding typed-objects with relationships and properties following an underlying objectified relational data 
structure. Versions progressed from basic geometry toward integrated representations of broader aspects like construc-
tion schedules, structural analysis models and sustainability metrics.
IFC defines three primary layer categories: Resource, Core and Interoperability [110]. The Resource layer manages 
generic non-geometric data like materials or units. The Core layer contains high-level objects like buildings and spaces 
along with relationships between components. Interoperability extends specific properties for domains like structural 
analysis or cost estimation. IFC also adopts an open-source approach allowing professionals and software vendors to 
contribute expansions following established procedures [111].
IFC classifies objects hierarchically containing common general information independently inherited down to refined 
subtypes facilitating encoding of any building element [73]. For example, the IfcBuildingElement superclass constitutes all 
building parts with specific subclasses like IfcBeam or IfcSlab holding customized attributes. Particular objects’ intended 
use, relationships and properties are encoded through attributes assigned using controlled key sets. Property sets enable 
incorporating domain-specific data.
Unique identifiers (GUIDs) distinguish objects from one another avoiding ambiguity, even if representations differ 
between applications [112]. Quantities, material associations, connections, positioning and performance properties 
can all be encapsulated. Parametric constraints may also be described. The IFC schema serves as a neutral format, with 
software applications tasked to map native concepts to IFC classifications.
Areas requiring continued attention involve parametric modelling schemas, structural analysis model definitions, 
probabilistic/semantic representations of uncertainty and more expansive classification frameworks [108]. Emerging 
extensions target domains like geospatial relationships, roads and linear infrastructure, drainage and terrain modelling

6.2  Development of BIM collaboration platforms
Model-based infrastructures demand robust collaboration enabling dispersed teams synchronizing virtually across mile-

editing of persistent model compositions. Considerations around user workflows, scalability, security and server architectures 
impact success realizing next-generation cross-disciplinary practices.
6.2.1  Single‑model servers
Centralized model repositories optimize concurrent editing through live model exchange rather than isolated local work-
flows. Specialized BIM servers provision:
1.	 Model synchronization: Bidirectional model replication ensures geographically distributed users operate simultane-
ously on a consistent shared copy reducing merge conflicts.
2.	 Access management: Fine-grained permissions authorize user/group access centered on well-defined model seg-
ments matching assigned workflows/tasks.
3.	 Version control: Continuous model snapshots record revision histories enabling auditing, comparisons or rolling-back 
unintended overwrites without permanent data loss.
Representative products include Autodesk BIM 360 (formerly A360), Bentley ProjectWise and Trimble Tekla BIMsight 
championing synchronicity through high-availability global server infrastructures. Associated design coordination/review 
interfaces facilitate issue logging, markups and model viewing across organizations.
While optimizing real-time co-production, single centralized repositories concentrate computational loads and face single-
points-of-failure risks. Scalability proving robustness handling continent-scale production models remains unproven. Migrat-
ing legacy isolated workflows also demands cultural transitions leveraging model server potentials fully.
6.2.2  Distributed model frameworks
Alternatively, distributed model frameworks propagate live model exchanges directly between co-located clients without 
intermediary transaction servers. Tools like Assemble, BIMfuse and InfraWorks employ peer-to-peer replication enhancing 
scalability/resiliency at the expense of fine-grained centralized access controls.
Some software products have started incorporating blockchain technologies to provide a secure and transparent way of 
validating transaction logs and ensuring the integrity of models, even when they are distributed across different locations 
[129]. However, it is worth noting that certain platforms in this domain are still in their early stages of development and may 
not offer robust authorization management functionalities that are necessary for practical, real-world applications. Further-
more, the issue of conflict resolution poses a significant challenge in decentralized environments, where the lack of central-
ized coordination can hinder the efficient and effective resolution of conflicts that may arise during collaborative processes.
Overall, both server and distributed approaches optimize collaboration through live model synchronization suited for 
construction-scale infrastructures if scalable and secure. Standardized live model interfaces hiding network complexities 
from engineers focus on inherent model productivity potentials rather than native application functionality. Specialized 
model review interfaces tailored across expertise domains also enhances intuitive participation.

6.4  Risk assessment in BIM implementation
While BIM offers transformative advantages in bridge engineering, its implementation introduces risks that require care-
ful assessment and mitigation strategies:
1.	 Data Security Risks: The integration of IoT and cloud-based BIM platforms exposes projects to potential cybersecu-
rity threats. Unauthorized access to sensitive project data, such as design specifications or structural details, could 
compromise project integrity and stakeholder trust.
2.	 Project Delays: Inadequate training, resistance to change, or insufficient interoperability between platforms can lead 
to delays during the transition to BIM workflows. For instance, issues with data exchange standards such as IFC or 
misaligned software capabilities can disrupt collaboration and coordination.
3.	 Interoperability Failures: Vendor lock-in and incompatibilities between software tools can hinder data exchange 
and create inefficiencies, especially in multi-disciplinary projects. Without standardized workflows and interfaces, 
seamless collaboration remains a challenge.
4.	 Cost Overruns: The high initial investment in BIM software, hardware, and training can strain budgets, especially for 
smaller organizations or projects with limited resources.
To address these risks, organizations should implement robust cybersecurity protocols, invest in comprehensive train-
ing programs, and adopt standardized data formats such as IFC. Conducting pilot projects to identify interoperability 
issues early and gradually scaling BIM adoption can also mitigate implementation challenges. Effective risk management 
ensures that BIM can realize its full potential in transforming bridge engineering.

Abstract: This paper reviewed the application of parametric building information modelling (BIM) in bridge engineering, highlight- ing its contributions to improving workflows, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration, enhancing interoperability, and optimizing design processes. It examined how parametric modeling facilitated rapid design exploration and simulation- driven optimization through flexible, rule-based relationships. Case studies illustrated the use of parametric techniques to create customizable bridge components and assemblies, which enhanced decision-making through seamless integration with analysis tools. Furthermore, this study discussed forward design, an emerging trend that improved collaboration efficiency and cost control by establishing early computational definitions, as opposed to following traditional document- driven design methods. It also emphasized the importance of open standards, such as Industry Foundation Classes (IFC), for information exchange, noting the need to extend these standards for specialized infrastructure domains. Finally, it outlined future research directions, including scalability, multimodal data integration, and generative design, aiming to fully leverage the potential of BIM throughout the lifecycle of bridges. Highlights • Parametric BIM boosts teamwork and speeds up bridge design, leading to more efficient construction processes. • Customizable bridge components allow for better decision-making and integration with engineering analysis tools. • Open standards can enhance information sharing, paving the way for more innovative bridge design approaches.
